qs.q: A newborn is diagnosed with craniosynostosis involving the bilateral premature closure of the coronal suture. Which clinical anomaly is classically associated with this specific suture closure pattern?
qs.e: Bilateral premature closure of the coronal suture is associated with brachydactyly, whereas unilateral premature closure of the coronal suture is associated with plagiocephaly.
qs.s: Review — Skin, Embryology, Spine & Skull: MCQs

faq.a: No; plagiocephaly is molding of a normal suture. Persistent asymmetry warrants imaging to rule out true synostosis.
faq.q: Can positional plagiocephaly progress to craniosynostosis?

faq.a: The skull is most pliable and the brain is still expanding, allowing better remodeling with less blood loss.
faq.q: Why is surgery performed before 1 year of age?

faq.a: Use high‑quality skull X‑rays and detailed clinical assessment; refer to a center with CT if surgical planning is uncertain.
faq.q: What if CT is not available?

exam: A 4‑month‑old presents with a narrow head and a palpable midline ridge. What is your next diagnostic step and why? — Perform a skull X‑ray to confirm sagittal suture fusion; CT is ideal but not essential initially.

How does unilateral coronal synostosis differ clinically from positional plagiocephaly? — Fixed frontal bossing and ear shift on the affected side versus soft‑tissue molding that improves with repositioning.
A child with known Crouzon syndrome shows papilledema. What immediate management is required? — Urgent decompressive surgery or ventriculostomy to lower ICP before definitive cranial remodeling.

Why is vitamin D supplementation important before operating on a child with craniosynostosis in a tropical setting? — Deficiency can cause rickets‑related bone weakness, increasing intra‑operative fracture risk and poor healing.

What are the key intra‑operative considerations for a low‑resource hospital performing cranial vault remodeling? — Minimise blood loss (use tranexamic acid if available), maintain normothermia, provide prophylactic antibiotics, and have a blood transfusion plan.

Explain how you would differentiate hydrocephalus from craniosynostosis on examination. — Hydrocephalus shows a rapidly enlarging, tense fontanelle with no suture ridge; craniosynostosis has a fixed ridge and abnormal head shape.

A mother with untreated hyperthyroidism delivers a baby with trigonocephaly. How does maternal disease relate to the infant’s condition? — Excess maternal thyroid hormone can accelerate fetal bone maturation, predisposing to early suture closure.

What follow‑up schedule would you advise after successful vault remodeling in a low‑resource setting? — Head circumference every 2‑3 months, developmental checks every 6 months, and repeat imaging only if clinical concerns arise.
ai.title: Craniosynostosis
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: Premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures restricts skull growth, causing abnormal head shape and possible neurodevelopmental compromise. Diagnosis relies on clinical exam and imaging; management is surgical reshaping, tailored to severity and resources.

b: Diagnosed by characteristic head shape and palpable ridge over fused suture
Confirmatory imaging: plain skull X‑ray or low‑dose CT (3‑D reconstruction preferred)
Exclude secondary causes (metabolic, infectious) with basic labs when possible
sections.p: Craniosynostosis is the pathologic early fusion of a cranial suture before the brain has completed its rapid growth phase, leading to restricted skull expansion perpendicular to the fused suture.

b: Single‑suture (mild) vs. multi‑suture (moderate) vs. pansynostosis (severe)
ICP signs (bulging fontanelle, vomiting, papilledema) upstage to urgent surgery
sections.p: Severity is staged by the number of sutures involved and the presence of raised intracranial pressure (ICP) or neurodevelopmental delay.

b: Idiopathic (≈ 80 %): no identifiable genetic or systemic cause
Syndromic (e.g., Crouzon, Apert, Pfeiffer) – often autosomal dominant FGFR mutations
Acquired: intra‑uterine infections (CMV, rubella), maternal hyperthyroidism, severe vitamin D deficiency, untreated rickets
Tropical considerations: chronic malaria‑related anemia, sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusion affecting bone remodeling
sections.p: Most cases are idiopathic, but several syndromic and acquired factors are relevant, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Sagittal synostosis → scaphocephaly (long, narrow head)
Coronal synostosis → brachycephaly (short, wide head) or plagiocephaly if unilateral
Metopic synostosis → trigonocephaly (triangular forehead)
Lambdoid synostosis → posterior plagiocephaly (asymmetrical occiput)
Developmental delay or seizures if ICP rises
sections.p: Presentation varies with the fused suture; the skull shape is the most obvious clue, often noticed by parents or during routine immunisation visits.

t.b: Which suture is fused? – Palpable ridge, abnormal head circumference, facial asymmetry
Is there a radiographic suture line? – Absence confirms fusion; useful where CT unavailable
What is the exact suture involvement and brain volume? – Precise surgical planning; if CT not available, rely on X‑ray + clinical pattern
Is there papilledema? – Indicates raised ICP, prompting urgent surgery

t.a: Basic labs (CBC, calcium, phosphate, thyroid function)
t.b: Are there metabolic contributors? – Treat hyperthyroidism or rickets before surgery; if labs unavailable, treat clinically suspected causes

b: Rapidly increasing head circumference
Persistent vomiting, irritability, seizures
Papilledema or optic atrophy
Progressive developmental delay
sections.p: Complications arise from restricted brain growth and increased ICP.

b: Early surgery (6‑12 months) for single‑suture disease – allows remodeling with minimal blood loss
Multisuture or pansynostosis – staged cranial vault remodeling, often after 12 months
If raised ICP: urgent decompressive craniectomy or ventriculostomy before definitive reshaping
Treat underlying metabolic issues first (e.g., give vitamin D for rickets, control hyperthyroidism)
Peri‑operative antibiotics (cefazolin) – prophylaxis; avoid aminoglycosides if renal function uncertain
Analgesia with paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs if coagulopathy suspected
sections.p: Surgical correction is definitive; timing balances brain growth potential with risk of neuro‑damage.

b: Serial head‑circumference measurements every 2‑3 months until 2 years
Developmental screening at 6‑month intervals
Repeat imaging only if head shape changes or ICP signs recur
Counselling families on early detection of abnormal head shape in future pregnancies
sections.p: Long‑term monitoring focuses on neurodevelopment and skull growth.

b: Positional plagiocephaly – soft‑spot molding, no suture fusion; improves with repositioning
Hydrocephalus – enlarged head from CSF accumulation, not suture closure
Microcephaly – overall small head, not due to suture fusion
sections.p: Conditions that produce abnormal head shape but have different pathophysiology.

b: Plain X‑ray may miss early suture fusion; CT is more sensitive
Papilledema can be absent early despite raised ICP; rely on clinical picture
Vitamin D deficiency can mask rickets‑related skull changes; check labs if possible
sections.p: Imaging and clinical signs may be deceptive in low‑resource settings.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid head growth with vomiting or seizures
